title: If EdTech Products Are Expensive, Ineffective, and Extractive, Why Are We Still Using Them?
author: Abby Rubin and Emily Cherkin
summary: School board director Abby Rubin and educator/writer Emily Cherkin make the case that EdTech in schools is expensive, ineffective, and extractive -- yet persists through institutional inertia and vendor lobbying rather than evidence. Nearly 90% of American public schools provide one-to-one devices, yet national NAEP scores remain below 2019 pre-pandemic levels, Pennsylvania 8th-graders are 60%+ below proficiency, and research suggests EdTech is widening achievement gaps rather than closing them. Attention costs are severe: students are off-task on classroom devices as much as 38 minutes per hour. The 2025 FTC COPPA clarification holds that schools cannot consent to student data collection on behalf of parents -- yet most EdTech products collect data without explicit parental consent. Digital citizenship resources from Common Sense Media and ISTE carry conflicts of interest through Google and Chan-Zuckerberg funding. The 'digital test prep' justification fails scrutiny (digital tests don't require digital classrooms). The authors call for parental opt-out rights until EdTech is independently shown to be safe, effective, legal, and demonstrably superior to traditional instruction.
points: * Nearly 90% of U.S. public schools provide one-to-one devices, yet achievement scores remain below 2019 pre-pandemic levels and research suggests EdTech widens rather than closes the achievement gap. * Students are off-task on classroom devices as much as 38 minutes of every hour; 29% of teens used ChatGPT to answer math questions in 2025 -- when given a homework machine, students use it. * The FTC's 2025 COPPA update clarified that schools cannot consent to data collection on behalf of parents -- a protection the vast majority of EdTech products are violating. * Digital citizenship resources from Common Sense Media and ISTE should be scrutinized for conflicts of interest: both receive funding from Google, the Chan-Zuckerberg Foundation, and other EdTech interests. * The case for parental opt-out: until EdTech is independently shown to be safe, effective, legal, and demonstrably superior to traditional instruction, parents must be given the right to return to teacher-led models.
quotes: In 2013, Bill Gates optimistically said, 'We won't know for ten years' if investing in educational technology (EdTech) will improve learning. Now, in 2026, there is growing concern about the disconnect between how students learn and how they are being taught.
One study suggests that students using classroom devices are off-task as much as 38 minutes of every hour.
When children are given a homework machine, it should not be surprising when they use it.
Privacy invasion is another, even more pernicious -- and often hidden -- problem with EdTech products.

Until EdTech is independently shown to be safe, effective, legal, and demonstrably superior to traditional instruction, parents must be given the right to opt out, and instead, opt back into a teacher-led model.
